title: SQL Injection
subtitle: How attackers turn input fields into database commands — and how parameterized queries stop them completely

content.text: SQL injection (SQLi) happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL query without sanitisation. The attacker's input becomes part of the query's logic — not just a value, but a command. It has been in every OWASP Top 10 since the list began (now under A03 — Injection). A single SQLi vulnerability can result in full database read access, data modification, authentication bypass, and sometimes OS command execution.

content.filename: Prisma and Drizzle — safe by default

content.text: Defence in depth for SQL injection

content.code:
LAYER 1 — Parameterized queries (primary defence, mandatory)
  Never concatenate user input into SQL. Always use ? or $1 placeholders.

LAYER 2 — Least privilege database user
  Your app's DB user should only have SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
  It should NOT have DROP TABLE, CREATE USER, FILE (reads OS files)
  Limits damage if injection occurs

LAYER 3 — Input validation
  If an ID should be a number: verify it's a number before the query
  parseInt(id) === NaN → reject the request
  But don't rely on this as your primary defence — validate AND parameterize

LAYER 4 — Error handling — don't leak schema
  NEVER return raw database errors to users:
  'ERROR: column "usernaem" does not exist at character 42' tells attacker
  your schema, column names, and DB type
  Return generic error messages; log the full error server-side only

LAYER 5 — WAF (Web Application Firewall)
  Cloudflare and AWS WAF can detect and block common SQLi patterns
  Not a replacement for parameterized queries — a last line of defence

content.text: Input escaping is NOT a sufficient defence. You may have seen advice to 'escape user input' (replacing quotes with escaped quotes). This approach is fragile — different databases have different escaping rules, escaping can be bypassed in multi-byte character encodings, and it only works for certain injection contexts (string values, not identifiers). Parameterized queries separate the SQL command from the data at the protocol level — they are the only reliable defence.

questions.question: A developer validates that req.query.id is a number before using it: 'const id = parseInt(req.query.id); const q = `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ${id}`'. Is this safe?
options: Yes — since id is confirmed to be a number, concatenation is safe
Yes — parseInt prevents any string injection
No — validation reduces the attack surface but still allows numeric-based injection techniques like UNION attacks
No — it's still vulnerable because parseInt could return NaN which gets into the query
questions.explanation: In this specific case — an integer ID validated with parseInt — the concatenation is actually safe, because a number can never contain SQL metacharacters. However, this is a fragile pattern that breaks immediately for any other data type (strings, emails, names). The correct approach is always a parameterized query: 'db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1", [id])'. This works for all types, is immune to all SQL injection techniques, and is readable. Relying on type validation as a security control is a habit that leads to vulnerabilities when requirements change.

faq.a: Yes — 'NoSQL injection' is different from SQL injection but real. MongoDB queries are JavaScript objects: if you take user input and directly use it as a query filter, an attacker can inject query operators. Example: { password: { $gt: '' } } — the $gt operator matches all non-empty passwords, bypassing login. Defence: use Mongoose (which sanitizes input) or manually validate that query values are strings/numbers, not objects.

examples: Sony Pictures (2011) was breached via SQL injection in a fan site. Attackers extracted the personal data of 1 million users, including plaintext passwords (another problem), internal documents, and unreleased films. The breach used a union-based SQL injection on a search field

SQLMap is an open-source tool that automates SQL injection detection and exploitation. A security researcher can point it at any URL and it will automatically test dozens of injection techniques. If your app is vulnerable, a non-expert attacker can find it in minutes using automated tools
